title: 7. Water and Intention: The Anatomy of Ablution
purpose: It sets out the legal anatomy of purity — what nullifies ablution, and the sevenfold obligations and twelvefold practices of both the lesser and greater purity — as the second pillar after walaya, drawing on Ismaili juridical and majalis sources.

points.text: A Question-and-Answer book arranged on the order of the doors of Daaim al-Islam, containing questions from teachers of the Indian lands and answers from the summoners (duat) of the Yemeni lands, is cited as an authority on purity.

Asked whether the prohibition on urinating beneath fruit-bearing trees means trees actually bearing fruit or trees whose property it is to bear fruit, the Yemeni respondents answer that it covers both.

Though the dawah books forbid greeting or speaking to one in a state of hadath, the answer given is that once he has risen from that place (having cleansed himself with a stone or otherwise) he may be greeted, must return the greeting, and may speak.
Reusing a stone or clod of earth used for cleansing after urination is permitted once it has dried, provided no impurity and no moisture are evident upon it.

Mukhtasar al-Musannaf lists the nullifiers of ablution as sleep, whatever issues from the front or rear passage (including a stone or wind), an enema, fainting, insanity, and the disappearance of the glans into the front passage of a living or dead person.

Tawil al-Daaim reports that one who interrupts his ablution may build upon what he has already done, so long as the water has not dried upon the limbs already washed; and Mukhtasar al-Musannaf holds that one whose hands are amputated above the elbows is relieved of the obligation to wash them.

The Trusted of the Imam, the Banner of Islam, in the fifth council of Majalis al-Bayan and Majalis al-Hikma (the Councils of al-Mustansiriyya), teaches that each of the seven obligations of Islam itself contains seven obligations and twelve practices, mirroring the honored number nineteen formed from the testimony's seven and twelve letters.
Walaya is the first and most excellent of the obligations, and in every allusion made by these numbers the ranking of the friends of God is the utmost aim and intention.

Purity follows walaya in rank, and its lesser purity (ablution) has seven obligations: pure water, intention, washing the face, washing the hands, wiping the head, wiping the feet, and order — beginning with what God began by mentioning.

The twelve practices (sunan) of ablution are istinja, washing the hands before entering the vessel, pronouncing God's name on sitting down, rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, moving the ring, combing water through the beard, wetting the eyes, giving the right precedence over the left, wiping the inner and outer ears, the second and third washings of the face (the first being the obligation), and the siwak.

The greater purity — washing of the whole body — likewise has seven obligations: washing from janabah, from menstruation, of the unbeliever entering Islam, of one recovering from unconsciousness, from the blood of nifas, after immersion in impurity, and of the dead, which is an obligation upon the living until one of them performs it.

The twelve practices of the greater purity are the washings of Friday, of Eid al-Fitr, of Eid al-Adha, for ihram, for entering the Haram, the Kabah, and Madinah, on the day of Arafah, on the nights of the nineteenth, twenty-first and twenty-third of Ramadan, and after washing the dead.

Ali ibn Abi Talib, in his four hundred maxims of conduct, commands cleansing with water from foul odor, prescribes invocations on entering the privy and on looking at what has passed, and states that when sleep mingles with the heart ablution becomes obligatory.
